thread.title: Glencore: Providing The Cobalt Tech That Car Companies Need To Survive - Glencore Plc (OTCMKTS:GLCNF)

author: Ezra Weener
title: Glencore: Providing The Cobalt Tech That Car Companies Need To Survive - Glencore Plc (OTCMKTS:GLCNF)
text:
Intro: As the electric vehicle age is storming in, there are clear investment strategies to take advantage of it. In this article, I want to look at one specific resource that will be incredibly necessary and the company that I believe is best positioned to supply it when demand increases: Cobalt and Glencore ( OTCPK:GLCNF ) respectively. I also look into the effects it will have on other industries such as the smartphone industry and the moves Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) is making to combat it.
To give some background, Cobalt is a metal that is traded as a commodity and it tends to be mined as a byproduct of mining nickel and copper. It is used as an essential material in the batteries used in many phones and electric cars. Due to the huge increase in demand in recent years and demand expectations in the future, the price has soared. In the last two years, it has nearly tripled in price.
Reason For Increased Demand As the EV market gets larger, the demand for cobalt will grow. As this happens, with the current meager production, many companies from phone producers to car manufacturers will be looking for cobalt, and Glencore is the world's largest producer. Not only is the company the largest producer of cobalt, but the company plans to expand its cobalt production 133% in the next three years, according to their annual filing last year. This would make them the largest producer in the world by a significant margin. As demand increases, the potential profits are large.
The reason cobalt is so necessary is because it adds stability to lithium-ion batteries that tend to be lost when battery density increases. This means that cobalt raises the amount of charge a battery can hold before it becomes unstable. With the size of batteries and the amount we need them to do, energy density is one of the most important factors for battery production and it relies heavily on cobalt.
The resource is in no way abundant. Glencore, the largest producer in the world mined only 7kt of cobalt in the first quarter, compare that to the over 1,000 times more silver they mined in the same quarter. It currently barely makes a dent on their income statement but over time likely will become very relevant.
Political Barriers : In addition to just mining the metal, the cobalt industry struggles with transparency and human rights violations as ⅔ of the world's cobalt is mined in Congo. There have been significant abuses of workers and allegations of terrible working conditions . Companies working there also are often forced to do business with corrupt politicians and less than ideal people. Glencore has begun getting all their affairs in order in Congo , which is necessary to do succeed in the country.
While historically, this difficulty doing business in the DRC has been a risk for the company, as demand for cobalt grows, it could also become an asset. The choppy waters of the DRC would make it incredibly difficult for new companies to start cobalt production and also adds a level of deterrence for old companies looking to expand their operations. As Glencore has already stated their increased goals in terms of level of production, it is clear they find it completely likely that their own goals of expansion should not be a problem. While they will be expanding to help meet supply, it will be hard for other companies to follow suit to the degree that could cause a potential glut. While many commodities that boom in price ends up seeing price deflation due to oversupply within a few years, this seems unlikely for cobalt.
The difficulty, however, lies in the murkiness of the waters. On July 2nd, the company got hit with a subpoena looking into money-laundering and bribery charges that sent the stock tumbling. While there is definite risk in this space as the company has had to make settlements with sanctioned businessmen and having stakes in sanctioned companies. However, while we must await the outcomes, as a large-scale bribery charge could be harmful to foreign operations, especially if any sanctions are levied, the company has a strong balance sheet and the global operations to maintain steadiness throughout the process. In addition, the company has issued a share buyback immediately after tumbling, a likely sign it believes the price movement is overblown. However, this is a risk that must be watched and managed for this to be a good investment as there is large downside risk.
It is likely in the next few years we will see much higher levels of mining in Australia; many junior miners have already started looking to start or expand operations there . However, the cobalt in Australia is less economical to mine and many of these miners have long ways until they even decide whether it is an endeavor worth pursuing. That being said, with the political and ethical questions in the DRC, Australian cobalt could help answer the need for clean sourcing of the material . However, if that is to happen, it is likely years down the road and will still be less economical than the DRC.
Glencore has large operations in the DRC and small operations (in terms of cobalt production) in Australia. In the DRC, they have two main sources, the primary cobalt production comes from these two assets: Katanga Copper-Cobalt mine as well as Mutanda Copper-Cobalt mine. In Australia, the small cobalt production comes from a nickel asset: Murrin Murrin. I have included mine by mine analysis for the production of cobalt at both Katanga and Murrin Murrin at the bottom.
Tech's Need For Cobalt: The need for cobalt is clear to both producers and consumers. Many of the largest electronics manufacturers have scrambled to guarantee their cobalt supplies ahead of imminent scarcity. Apple, for example, has worked hard to try to source their cobalt directly from miners , a move clearly out of direct necessity as usually they would allow their own battery manufacturers to buy the material themselves. This is because as stated in the sourced article, Apple is one of the world's largest end-user consumers of cobalt, a supply directly necessary to their phones. Without proper supply, this could put a bottleneck on the quantity of phones the company can produce.
We have seen similar trends for auto manufacturers. This makes sense as the amount of cobalt necessary for a car battery, at around 8kg, is over 1,000 time the amount needed for a phone battery. Volkswagen ( OTCPK:VLKAY ) and BMW ( OTCPK:BMWYY ) have both tried directly sourcing cobalt to try to ensure their supplies. While some companies such as Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA ) and Apple are currently trying to avoid buying DRC cobalt as it is unethically sourced, as demand grows, the other markets will be unable to meet the supply needs: This has already started as Apple agreed to source its cobalt from the DRC and Samsung ( OTC:SSNLF ) is following suit.
Glencore itself has entered a deal to provide nearly a third of its current cobalt production to a Chinese battery recycler GEM as they have been unable to maintain their supply from just recycled material. As the article states, this is significant because there is very little clean cobalt in the world to go around, so guaranteeing supply is important. The company understands this and does more than just producing cobalt. It also is in the business of recycling and marketing cobalt .
Effect On Earnings: Due to these trends, Glencore has put a large emphasis on being the company to meet much of the increased demand for the product. The company has stated its goal to produce 133% more cobalt over the next three years. In the first quarter, they produced 7kt of cobalt, an 11% increase YoY. This increase of 7kt is worth $55M on the market today. The company produce 27kt in 2017 and is looking to produce 63kt by 2020. At current prices, this would amount to $5.04B worth of revenue. This may not seem like that much revenue in comparison to the $210B of revenue earned in 2017, but if prices continue to soar, this could be an even larger area of growth. This does not take into account the increases in copper and nickel also needed for lithium batteries needed for the EV expansion as shown in the second graphic. As the company gears up production for those materials to achieve production increases of 25% for copper and 30% for nickel, these should have even larger impacts on the income statement as these materials currently account for $19B of revenue.

Balance Sheet: The company has a strengthening balance sheet and has improved operations. As can be seen by the graphic below, the company has increased earnings while decreasing debt and improving its balance sheet. The company as can be seen by its FFO/debt should have no problem meeting any of its obligations. The company has used this to invest $4.234B in capital expenditures in 2017 - 21% higher than 2016.
Mines:
For the Katanga mine , Glencore's largest source of Cobalt, Glencore is an 86.3% stakeholder. The mine had undergone work, one of the reasons for reduced production before ramping up for the near future. As the company said in its 1Q18 10-Q, "On September 11, 2015, the Company announced the decision to suspend the processing of copper and cobalt during the construction phase of the Whole Ore Leach ("WOL") project (the "WOL Project"). The suspension continued throughout most of 2017 with copper production resuming on December 11, 2017. Cobalt production resumed on March 7, 2018. The WOL Project includes the construction of optimized copper and cobalt circuits intended to reliably produce 300,000 tpa of copper cathode and 40,000 tpa of cobalt contained in hydroxide over life of mine". Production has started as progress according to the project schedule is being made on the cobalt debottlenecking project and cobalt dryers (the "Cobalt Projects") aimed at increasing maximum cobalt production capacity to 40,000 tonnes per annum by Q1 2019. In addition, the statement says, "Due to operational challenges experienced during cobalt commissioning, no cobalt hydroxide had cleared the DRC border as at March 31, 2018, leading to nil cobalt sales in Q1 2018. Cobalt has subsequently cleared the border with sales commencing in April 2018." All the signs point to this mine hitting full stride in no time. In addition, the company put $12.3m into capital expenditures for the cobalt projects in this mine.
To compare to the 40kt expected by Katanga mine, the Australian operation (Murrin Murrin), which produces cobalt metal as a byproduct of nickel instead of copper, only produces .2kt per year.
Investment: The company has just received a subpoena for bribery charges and has had its stock price tumble over 5% in the last couple days which put the company into a value category despite its possible growth position. The company has strong operations and has significant growth opportunities in incredibly important materials that will be essential to large industries in upcoming years. The company has a very strong balance sheet that is only getting stronger. There is much room to grow and now is the best time to invest.
